A spaniel is a type of dog — not a single specific breed, but a whole group of dog breeds that share certain physical features and personality traits. Think of it like how "terrier" or "hound" refers to a family of related dogs. A spaniel is one such family.

Spaniels are easy to recognize once you know what to look for. They tend to be small to medium-sized dogs with:

  • Long, floppy ears that hang down on the sides of their face — this is probably their most recognizable feature.
  • Soft, wavy or silky fur, often with longer, feathery hair on their ears, chest, legs, and tail.
  • Large, round, soulful eyes that give them a gentle, almost melting expression — the kind of look that makes people feel immediately warm toward them.
  • A sturdy but graceful body, built for movement through fields, water, and undergrowth.
What spaniels are like in personality

Spaniels are known for being affectionate, eager to please, loyal, and lively. They love being around people and are generally very friendly — with their owners, with strangers, and often with other animals too. They are energetic and enjoy exercise, but they are also happy to curl up close to a person they love.

Because of these traits, spaniels are considered excellent companion dogs and family pets. They are sensitive animals — they respond well to kindness and can become anxious or withdrawn if treated harshly.
What spaniels were originally bred to do

Spaniels were originally working dogs, bred centuries ago to help hunters. Their job had two main parts:

  1. Flushing — running through dense undergrowth, bushes, or tall grass to disturb and drive out birds (like pheasants or woodcock) hiding there, so the hunter could shoot them.
  2. Retrieving — fetching the shot birds and bringing them back to the hunter, often from water, since many spaniels are strong swimmers.

This hunting background explains why spaniels are energetic, have a keen nose, and love to explore their surroundings. Even pet spaniels today often show instincts like sniffing everything thoroughly or darting after birds.

Since "spaniel" is a group, there are many individual breeds within it. Some of the most well-known are:

  • Cocker Spaniel — one of the most popular and well-loved, known for its sweet temperament and silky coat. There are two varieties: the English Cocker Spaniel and the American Cocker Spaniel (slightly smaller, with a rounder head and more abundant fur).
  • Cavalier King Charles Spaniel — a very small, gentle, and deeply affectionate breed, often considered among the most loving of all dog breeds. Historically a lapdog of royalty.
  • English Springer Spaniel — larger and more athletic than a Cocker Spaniel, with great energy and a strong instinct for fieldwork.
  • Field Spaniel, Clumber Spaniel, Sussex Spaniel, Welsh Springer Spaniel — less common varieties, each with their own distinct look and character, but all part of the same family.

Despite their differences in size and appearance, all these breeds share the essential "spaniel" traits: the ears, the coat, the temperament, and the working instinct.

Today, most spaniels are kept as companion animals rather than hunting dogs. They fit well into family life because they are gentle with children, sociable, and not aggressive. However, they do need regular exercise and mental stimulation — a bored spaniel can become anxious or destructive. Their long ears and silky coats also require regular cleaning and grooming to stay healthy.
The figurative use of the word

Outside of its literal meaning, "spaniel" is sometimes used figuratively in English — usually in literature or formal writing — to describe a person who is excessively servile or fawning: someone who follows another person around eagerly, trying to please them at every turn, almost embarrassingly so.

This usage draws directly from the dog's nature. A spaniel is devoted and eager to please its master. So calling a person a "spaniel" (or saying they behave like one) suggests they are overly submissive, lacking in dignity, and desperate for approval or favor from someone more powerful. This figurative sense carries a mildly contemptuous tone — it implies the person has surrendered their own self-respect.

This metaphorical use appears in Shakespeare and other classic literature, so you may encounter it in older texts.

A spaniel is a group of dog breeds characterized by long floppy ears, a soft silky coat, and a gentle, loyal, eager-to-please nature — originally bred as hunting dogs, now mostly beloved as companion animals — and the word can also be used figuratively to describe a person who is obsequiously devoted to another.
